Summary
This chapter examined the essential building blocks of data architectures in Azure, mapping core
capabilities—such as ingestion, processing, storage, and serving—to corresponding Azure services.
We explored how these capabilities support established patterns such as Lambda, Kappa, and
Medallion, and how services such as Azure Databricks, Synapse Analytics, Event Hubs, Stream
Analytics, and Data Explorer play distinct roles depending on the scenario.
We also covered HTAP, identifying Synapse Link for Cosmos DB as the only Azure-native service
that currently enables real-time analytics directly on transactional data without data duplication
between the OLTP and OLAP systems.

Beyond platform services, we reviewed infrastructure enablers such as the SHIR, MVN, and VNDG
to bridge secure connectivity gaps between cloud and on-premises or private environments.
The use of Cosmos DB as a flagship OLTP store was also explored in detail through an example
of a multi-tenant mobile app for managing wine cellars, emphasizing best practices such as
partitioning, indexing strategy, and leveraging change feed for aggregate updates.
The chapter concluded with a retail use case involving smart fridges. A Kappa architecture was
implemented using Terraform and .NET, with telemetry ingested through Event Hubs, processed
in real time with Stream Analytics, and stored in Azure Data Explorer. Anomalies were forwarded
to an Azure function for alerting, illustrating a complete, scalable IoT analytics pipeline.

Artificial Intelligence
Architecture
This chapter is arguably the most challenging, given the inherently complex and fast-evolving
nature of AI, making it difficult to provide insights that will remain relevant over time. To address
this, we will concentrate on foundational concepts that are less likely to undergo significant
changes in the months and years ahead. This should help guide your future design decisions.
We will begin by distinguishing between generative and non-generative AI (traditional), high -
lighting scenarios where traditional AI remains the appropriate choice. We will then shift our
focus to Generative AI (GenAI), exploring both well-established patterns and emerging but
future-proof ones.
More specifically, we’ll look at the following topics:
• The AI Architecture Map
• Zooming in on traditional AI
• Zooming in on generative AI
Our use case will focus on the design aspects, as any provided code would likely become outdated
before the book is even published. Instead, the next chapter will provide a list of useful reference
implementations to help you progress in your AI journey.

Let’s get started with the traditional AI services
Zooming in on traditional AI services
You might ask why traditional AI services are still relevant in the age of GenAI. There are several
good reasons. GenAI’s creative outputs aren’t always appropriate, and the computational demands
of hosting Large Language Models (LLMs) can be significant, although Small Language Models
(SLMs) are less demanding. In contrast, traditional AI offers more predictable results and is often
a far more cost-effective solution.
When dealing with business cases that demand high precision, have a well-defined scope, and
require minimal custom training, traditional AI remains a strong candidate.
Most Azure AI services support custom training with your own data—whether it’s text, images,
or audio—enabling the resulting models to perform effectively in real-world situations.
Figure 8.2 illustrates the traditional AI services that are part of Azure.

The diagram in Figure 8.2 has a few subsections, among which is Machine Learning.
Machine learning
Azure Machine Learning (Azure ML), a native offering, is by far the AI service that requires the
most true AI expertise. It supports both supervised and unsupervised learning, enabling a wide
range of capabilities. While GenAI outperforms it in many areas, Azure ML remains a strong
choice for prediction-driven scenarios and unsupervised learning.
Supervised learning requires human-based labeled data. In a nutshell, labeling is the process of
assigning labels to raw data to help the model make predictions when inferencing. For example,
if you had to build a solution that helps your employees report IT incidents and automatically
detects the incident category based on the description, you could proceed with the following steps:
1. Collect historical data: You would extract historical data from your Information Tech -
nology Service Management (ITSM) database.
2. Prepare data: Begin by cleaning and organizing the data, as data quality is often subopti -
mal in most systems. Enhancing data quality is essential before training any model—after
all, as the saying goes, garbage in, garbage out.
3. Label prepared data: You would then assign a category to each incident description. This
labeled dataset would serve as the ground truth for training your model.
4. Train the model: You would choose the appropriate algorithm for training data. This

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition

could be one of the multiclass classification options.
5. Evaluate the model: The last step before launching the model and making it available to
applications would be to evaluate its accuracy and precision, using well-known techniques
such as precision, recall, and F-score.
Azure ML has tools that help accomplish and complete each of the preceding steps.
On the other hand, unsupervised learning doesn’t require data labeling as it involves looking at
patterns and deviations in behavior across a large dataset. If we look at the previous example, we
could extract our ITSM data and use unsupervised learning to identify patterns and outliers in data
clusters of IT incidents. This step could help clean our data before training our supervised model.
Today, with the rise of GenAI, Microsoft’s focus has shifted a bit, and many practitioners com -
plain about outdated examples and SDKs for Azure ML. A solid alternative is Azure Databricks,
especially if you are already using Spark.

Chapter 8 291
Natural language processing
You may not realize it but Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a very complex field of AI. Nat -
ural language is inherently ambiguous—it includes humor, irony, homonyms, polysemy, and
more. Even among humans, miscommunication is common. We often need to repeat ourselves
or clarify our intent by providing additional context.
The most challenging aspect of NLP is capturing semantics—that is, understanding the meaning
of words within their specific context. In traditional AI, we rely on techniques such as tokenization.
Tokens can represent entire words, subwords, or even individual characters such as punctuation
marks. AI models are trained on tokenized text and automatically break down our inputs into
tokens during processing. Tokenization is a fundamental technique used by every NLP practitioner.
However, tokens alone are not enough to extract semantics. A very popular NLP technique used to
extract semantics is Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging. This technique involves identifying words and
their grammatical roles within a sentence, and it remains relevant today. While tokens represent
individual, context-free segments of text, tags provide a more comprehensive understanding by
revealing the grammatical structure of the sentence.
For example, take the following sentence:
I am Stephane Eyskens, an Azure Cloud Architect.
The corresponding tags would be as follows:
"I" - Pronoun (PRP)
"am" - Verb (VBP)
"Stephane" - Noun (NNP)
"Eyskens" - Noun (NNP)
"," - Punctuation (",")
"an" - Determiner (DT)
"Azure" - Adjective (JJ)
"Cloud" - Noun (NN)
"Architect" - Noun (NN)
. (period) - Punctuation (PUNCT)
Once we have identified each word and its grammatical role in a sentence, we gain a deeper un -
derstanding of the text. Punctuation also plays a crucial role—symbols such as ., !, and ? help
indicate sentence boundaries, questions, and emphasis. POS tagging is often performed using
stochastic methods such as Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), which excel at predicting the most
likely sequence of letters, words, tags, or phonemes based on transition probabilities.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 292
However, we still need to refine the phrase further. For example, the word am in the preceding
sentence is derived from the verb to be, like many others, such as been, be, is, and was. To identify
the parent entity, we rely on the lemmatization technique, which helps reduce noise by identifying
the lemma of each word. Lemmatization applies not only to verbs but also to nouns, which can
have various forms depending on number, gender, and other factors. For instance, the lemma of
mice is mouse. In the preceding example, only the verb am differs from its base form. When com -
bined with POS tagging, lemmatization already provides a solid foundation for understanding

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 291
chunks.content:
the core meaning of a text.
Yet, the work doesn’t stop there. As mentioned earlier, language is inherently complex. A given
text may include proper nouns, such as names of people, cities, or countries, as well as concepts
such as project management —all of which are considered entities. Identifying these requires the
use of Named Entity Recognition (NER), a technique specifically designed to detect and classify
such elements in text.
NER identifies words or phrases in text that refer to specific, real-world concepts. For example,
Stephane Eyskens is a person, Azure is a cloud platform, and Cloud Architect is a job title—each
mapped to broader categories such as Person, Cloud Platform, and Job. NER remains a key compo -
nent of modern NLP pipelines, as recognized entities can be extracted from user input and passed
as parameters to downstream systems. For instance, with Azure’s Conversational Language
Understanding service, entities are automatically captured from a user query and forwarded to
the application code handling the request. This allows developers to define and train models to
extract custom entities, such as a ServiceNow ticket incident number. Even in a GenAI context,
entities are captured and passed as parameters to functions during a function-calling process.
All these NLP techniques are applied regardless of the end goal—whether it’s building conversa -
tional agents, performing sentiment analysis, or extracting keywords and key phrases from text.

Let’s explore another dimension, namely the realm of computer vision.
Optical character recognition, vision, and document
extraction
Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is the process of extracting text from images. For example,
your organization may handle a large volume of documents—such as PowerPoint files, PDFs, or
Visio diagrams—that include images containing embedded text (knowledge). You might also
receive scanned documents from customers or partners, such as invoices or purchase orders,
where text extraction is needed to enable automated processing. OCR is a computer vision task
that consists of interpreting each pixel in a given image to recognize text. Among the traditional
AI services, Azure ships with AI Vision and AI Custom Vision, which both are able to perform OCR
tasks but also image recognition to help categorize and classify images.
For example, you might self-host an instance of an AI Custom Vision model along with an IoT
Edge module used by cameras (IoT Edge devices) on industrial assembly lines to detect potential
product defects before packaging. In this scenario, you would train the Custom Vision model with
hundreds or even thousands of images, including both flawless and defective products. Once de -
ployed, the model performs real-time inferences on incoming images, classifying them based on
the training it received to flag anomalies as they occur on the production line. For general-purpose
vision requirements, you may rely on AI Vision alone.
AI Vision can be useful for extracting text from small, unstructured documents. However, for
scenarios involving semi-structured or larger documents, such as forms, invoices, or contracts,
you should consider using AI Document Intelligence, which is better suited for handling complex
layouts and extracting structured information at scale.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 294
AI Document Intelligence comes with predefined models that represent most document types.
Additionally, you can create custom extraction and classification models using Document In -
telligence Studio, to adhere to enterprise- and industry-specific documents. Classification is

appropriate processing service—especially if you support multiple document types.
Once the document type has been identified, you can extract its contents using a built-in or cus -

Document Intelligence is also very often used in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)-based

Other AI capabilities
Azure AI Search is a general-purpose search service increasingly used as a vector database and a
hybrid search engine, combining the strengths of both vector- and keyword-based search. While
Cosmos DB and Azure SQL also offer capabilities for full-text and vector search, Azure AI Search
remains the most versatile for search-centric scenarios. We will explain later in this chapter the
concept of a vector database and hybrid search.

We’re going to start with the enablers that will allow you to get started in your Azure AI journey.
GenAI enablers
Azure AI Foundry is a one-stop shop for all AI-related needs. It provides a unified portal where
users can explore a catalog of over 11,000 models, including a Microsoft-curated subset. These
curated models are production-ready and have undergone extensive internal compliance and
quality checks to meet enterprise standards. AI Foundry also allows you to select and test a model,
as well as evaluate its performance over time. The GitHub Marketplace is a free alternative that
offers similar features, though with usage limits enforced through throttling mechanisms.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 296
AI Foundry isn’t limited to the portal, as it also includes a full SDK to support the development of
intelligent applications. Microsoft’s complementary offering, the Semantic Kernel framework, is
available for free and provides developers with full flexibility in how they build AI-driven solutions.
Microsoft offers guidance at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/agents-sdk/
choose-agent-solution to help choose the most suitable solution based on the specific use case.
Semantic Kernel is an enterprise-grade, versatile framework that supports AI orchestration and
offers a wide range of connectors to vector databases. Organizations with a strong .NET footprint
often choose Semantic Kernel, while Python-based teams typically prefer LangChain due to its
native ecosystem integration. Python is the de facto programming language for data and AI, which
is why many data and AI engineers are exclusively proficient in Python.
In practice, developers from the .NET or Java ecosystem are generally accustomed to principles
such as SOLID, DRY, clean architecture, and clean code, which are deeply embedded in their devel -
opment culture. They are also very well acquainted with unit and integration testing. This is partly
due to the fact that .NET/Java were designed from the ground up as object-oriented platforms.
In contrast, Python, originally conceived as a scripting language, has historically encouraged a
more flexible and less rigid development style.
What I observed in the field is that, when building broader solutions that incorporate AI capabil -
ities, there can be a noticeable quality gap between deliverables produced by Python developers
and those by .NET/Java developers. This often stems from differing development practices, ar -
chitectural disciplines, and tooling standards inherent to each ecosystem.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 295
chunks.content:
That said, these are general trends rather than hard rules—you can find highly structured Python
developers as well as poorly disciplined .NET developers. Nevertheless, I felt it was important
to highlight this cultural difference, as it can lead to frictions and tensions between teams that
should not be underestimated. It’s also worth noting that Microsoft provides a Python SDK for
Semantic Kernel, offering teams the flexibility to adopt the framework regardless of their preferred
development language.
Important note
In August 2025, questions were raised about the future of Semantic Kernel, which
would transition from general availability to maintenance mode. Microsoft will focus
on a new framework. It’s worth following this GitHub issue: https://github.com/
microsoft/semantic-kernel/discussions/12779.

Chapter 8 297
Model capabilities
For any NLP scenario, Azure OpenAI’s GPT family is typically the best LLM choice. For cases that
have a well-defined scope, an SLM might be a preferred option. The Phi family is positioned as
a cost-friendly and performance-driven alternative. GPT-4o is the most advanced multimodal
model available through Azure OpenAI. It is also very proficient for code generation. Additionally,
it is the only model that features a real-time API for speech and audio.
Azure OpenAI also features speech-specific models across the TTS and Whisper families, as well
as vision-specific families such as DALL-E. Of course, many other models are made available
through AI Foundry, but we are focusing mostly on what’s available through Azure OpenAI.
The next section explores the infrastructure enablers that we can take advantage of to host and
build intelligent apps.
Infrastructure enablers
If you plan to run and orchestrate AI workloads within Kubernetes, the Kaito solution (https://
github.com/kaito-project/kaito) may be of great help. It is available as a managed add-on for
AKS. Kaito essentially helps deploy and run AI/ML models on Kubernetes clusters by handling
dynamic scaling and GPU demand at runtime.
Azure OpenAI models are made available in two different ways:
• Serverless endpoints: This deployment model is fully managed by Microsoft and follows
a pay-as-you-go token-based billing, typically measured in Tokens per Minute (TPM).
The TPM deployment model is subject to default subscription quotas, which can result
in throttling once those limits are reached.
• Provisioned throughput: This model is also fully managed but comes with reserved and
dedicated capacity. Cost and performance are predictable.
Other models can be deployed through the poorly named Managed Compute deployment model,
which is actually not managed by Microsoft but by the customer. It requires extra effort to get a
model ready for its first inference. Go for this if you want to control and manage the end-to-end
AI infrastructure or if you want to use a model that is not made available through Azure OpenAI.
The next section explores important topics that are commonly used in AI solutions.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 298
Embeddings generation, vector databases, and hybrid
search
We can’t talk about GenAI without explaining the concept of embeddings. The rise of deep learning
caused the widespread adoption of the text-embedding concept. Bidirectional Encoder Rep -
resentations from Transformers (BERT) is, among others, a transformer-based deep learning
model that is able to create embeddings, which are vector-based numeric representations, where
each number is a dimension. The number of dimensions you obtain depends on the model used
to generate the embeddings. In Azure OpenAI, there are a few models, such as text-embedding-

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 297
chunks.content:
ada-002, text-embedding-3-large, and text-embedding-3-small.
Other media types, such as images and audio, can be vectorized too, but let’s stick to text for now.
The purpose of text embeddings is to gather as much contextual information as possible and to
store it in the form of numeric vectors. Vectors can be compared with others to see whether they
look similar or not. Nowadays, we typically compare vectors by calculating their cosine similarity,
although other comparison techniques exist.
Embeddings support various use cases, including handling vague or ambiguous search queries.
Unlike keyword-based search, vector-based search considers the context of the query, enhancing
semantic understanding. This allows search engines—or any system processing natural language
queries—to retrieve more relevant results from a vector database.
Here is a small example that should help you understand the concept. The following two sen -
tences contain the word crane:
The construction supervisor leased a crane for the building project.
I learned about the migration patterns of the sandhill crane. These birds
are wonderful!
As human beings, we instantly identify the context and we understand that, despite crane being
the same word in both sentences, it has a totally different meaning because of the context in which
it is used. That is what transformers such as BERT help identify. BERT would capture the broader
context around the word crane. Let’s use Azure OpenAI to vectorize and calculate the cosine sim -
ilarity between our two sentences. We can run this piece of Python code (truncated for clarity):
print (cosine_similarity(
openai.Embedding.create(
input = "The construction supervisor leased a crane for the building
project.",

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 299
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 299
engine= "embedding")['data'][0]['embedding'],
openai.Embedding.create(
input = "I learned about the migration patterns of the sandhill crane.
These birds are wonderful!",
engine= "embedding")['data'][0]['embedding']))
With Azure OpenAI, the result of the preceding code is about 0.76, indicating a fairly high level
of similarity between the two sentences. A score near 0 suggests low to no similarity, while a
score near 1 indicates strong similarity. The exact score may vary depending on the model used
to generate the embeddings and the number of vector dimensions.
In traditional probabilities, a score of 0.76 is rather high, but this principle doesn’t apply to cosine
similarity. The cosine similarity score shouldn’t be treated as an absolute indicator of a true match
between two pieces of text. Instead, it’s more meaningful to sort scores in descending order and
focus on the highest ones to determine the most relevant matches. For example, let’s consider
the following sentences stored in a Python DataFrame and their corresponding vectors:
Figure 8.4 – Sentences and their corresponding vectors
Admittedly, these sentences are quite different and do not convey the same meaning. We can take
the top two results of a search query:
df["cs"] = df.ada_v2.apply(
lambda x: cosine_similarity(
x,
generate_embeddings(
"I'm looking for information about climate change?"
)
)
)
print (
df.sort_values("cs", ascending= False).head(2)
)
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 300
This would give us the closest matches, regardless of the actual value of the cosine similarity score.
Figure 8.5 – Search results using cosine similarity
A keyword-based method alone would be unlikely to return these results as the word climate
present in our query is not present in the data itself. The preceding examples demonstrate how to
compute embeddings and perform vector queries using a Python dataframe. In real-world scenar -
ios, however, the objective is to store vectors—representing the relevant knowledge domain—in
a persistent storage solution, such as a vector database, for future retrieval and use.
In Azure, several services can act as vector databases, enabling support for vector search queries.
One of the earliest was AI Search, which introduced hybrid search—a combination of vector-based
and keyword-based search capabilities. Although vector search offers greater semantic under -
standing, keyword search remains valuable in cases involving highly specialized terminology or
scenarios such as querying specific IT incident numbers and product identifiers.
However, Azure’s capabilities in this area have evolved rapidly, making hybrid search no longer a
key differentiator. Instead, you should choose a service based on other factors, such as scalability,
performance, and costs.

Ultimately, solution architecture is always about trade-offs—you need to weigh what matters

sustain. If you’re building a customer-facing chatbot embedded in a mobile app used by millions,
a high QPS capability becomes a top priority, potentially outweighing other factors. In our expe -
rience, the challenges we faced in most GenAI projects were not about AI itself but about how to
make it scalable, secure, and still affordable in terms of costs.
Let’s now explore a few AI patterns and use cases.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 302
Zooming in on AI patterns and use cases
Figure 8.6 illustrates the most common AI patterns and use cases:
Figure 8.6 – AI patterns and use cases
Before diving deeper into the patterns, let’s first examine the key concepts that underpin most
of them, namely, embeddings, vector databases, and hybrid search.
Retrieval augmentation generation
LLMs are trained on a huge amount of training data and parameters. However, they know noth -
ing about your data, unless that data was made public. To compensate for this, the RAG pattern
emerged and gained popularity shortly after the rise of GenAI. In essence, it enhances LLMs by
incorporating external knowledge—such as your organization’s data—into the generation pro -
cess. It has been particularly used in chat with your data scenarios, although it is not restricted to
chatbots. Figure 8.7 shows two variants of a RAG workflow.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 303
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 303
Figure 8.7 – RAG workflow
One way to achieve RAG for a chatbot is to follow these steps:
1. The user/system sends a query to the orchestration API.
2. The orchestration API retrieves the user query, converts it into a vector (embeddings), and
performs a search query against a vector database to find the closest matches (typically
using cosine similarity).
3. Next, the orchestration API forwards both the user query and the retrieved search results
to the LLM. The LLM evaluates whether the retrieved information aligns with the query
and then generates a coherent, human-readable response.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 304
The alternative approach involves first verifying whether the user’s initial query falls within the
chatbot’s scope before proceeding with the vector search. A possible Azure RAG architecture is
illustrated in Figure 8.8:
Figure 8.8 – Possible RAG architecture
The frontend talks to the chat API through Azure Application Gateway (the WAF) and Azure
API Management (APIM). The chat API queries the vector database (AI Search) and sends both
the results and the user query to the LLM through API Management, which plays the role of AI
gateway. Microsoft has published numerous policies that help deal with AI scenarios, such as
load balancing between LLM instances, dealing with token limits, and semantic caching. Ad -
ditionally, shielding the LLM from the rest of the world is a good practice as APIM can perform
some extra token validation —or apply any other policy—while authenticating to the LLM with
its managed identity.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 305
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 305
AI Search indexers can be used to crawl the prepared data available in a storage account, and we
can leverage AI Search’s built-in embedding skill capability to generate the embeddings. This skill
must be linked to an embedding model made available through a separate LLM instance. So, in
Figure 8.8, we use an instance for the conversation aspects and another one for the embedding
generation. For simple scenarios, the built-in embedding skill is good enough, and it is possible
to create a custom embedding skill for more advanced scenarios. One of the benefits of AI Search
as a vector database compared to other vector databases is the possibility of leveraging the in -
dexers to fill the vector indexes instead of having to push vector data ourselves. You may add an
extra component to the mix to store the conversation history and the possibility of resuming
older conversations.
From a code perspective, we can use Semantic Kernel, a Microsoft SDK, to deal with the conver -
sation orchestration and to abstract away the AI Search vector database using Semantic Kernel
vector stores. This abstraction layer makes it easy to switch to another vector database should
the application evolve.
Finally, Server-Sent Events (SSEs) can be used to stream tokens from the LLMs and progressively
display the response on the frontend, which is more user-friendly than waiting for the LLM to gen -
erate the full answer. As of June 2025, the GPT-4o Realtime API is in public preview and currently
supports only speech and audio, not text. Therefore, SSE remains the most effective approach for
streaming text responses. Naturally, this choice should be re-evaluated when considering how
best to interact with LLMs in the future.
It’s worth noting that the RAG pattern has several variants, including GraphRAG and LightRAG,
which aim to address some of the traditional limitations of standard RAG implementations—such
as limited contextual understanding and inefficiencies in retrieval and reasoning. Needless to say,
regardless of the chosen pattern, the quality of the source data plays a key role in the accuracy
of the RAG solution.
Let’s now explore another AI pattern.
Cache augmentation generation
One of the limitations of RAG is its reliance on a vector database with vector or hybrid search
capabilities. This retrieval step can introduce a performance overhead that may not always be
justified. While such a trade-off can be acceptable when working with hundreds of terabytes
of data, it becomes less desirable when dealing with smaller knowledge sets, where the cost of
retrieval may outweigh the benefits.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 306
The Cache Augmentation Generation (CAG) pattern is a good alternative as it eliminates the
need for a vector database or any other vector memory. It leverages the LLM’s large context win -

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 305
chunks.content:
dow to send the entire knowledge base to the LLM. A context window is the maximum number
of tokens LLMs can swallow in one go.
More specifically, we can override the LMM’s KV cache with our knowledge data, once and for
all. Any further interaction with the LLM will not require including extra context, and the LLM
alone is enough as it has the entire knowledge domain in its cache. Figure 8.9 provides a simpli -
fied view of CAG.
Figure 8.9 – CAG workflow
The first step consists of preparing the knowledge data and uploading it into the LLM’s KV cache.
The second and third steps simply interact with the LLM to query the knowledge domain. Some
open source frameworks make this possible, but as of June 2025, there is no true CAG support in
Azure. It is nevertheless interesting to be aware of the pattern as it can be a useful alternative to
RAG in some scenarios and could become available in the future.
CAG is particularly useful for smaller knowledge domains that can fit the context window of an
LLM. Beyond RAG and CAG, AI solutions often require extra tooling, which brings us to Tool-Aug -
mented Generation (TAG), our next pattern.
Tool-augmented generation
TAG has existed since the early days of GenAI. Its core purpose is to enhance an AI solution with
additional tools that enable it to perform actions. A practical example of this is GPT Actions in
ChatGPT. They allow you to define your own agent and connect it to custom APIs by importing
the OpenAPI definition into the action. Once configured, your custom GPT implementation can
autonomously interact with those APIs based on the prompts and logic you defined.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 307
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 307
Similarly, Azure OpenAI supports function calling —a technique that involves injecting a function
definition into the prompt and letting the LLM decide when it is appropriate to invoke it. For ex -
ample, when using Assistant Playground in AI Foundry, you can easily add a function like this one:
{
"name": "get_weather",
"description": "Determine weather in my location",
"parameters": {
"type": "object",
"properties": {
"location": {
"type": "string",
"description": "The city and state e.g. Seattle, WA"
},
"unit": {
"type": "string",
"enum": [
"c",
"f"
]
}
},
"required": [
"location"
]
},
"strict": false
}
In your first interaction with the LLM, you must inject this function signature through an appro -
priate prompt. The function signature makes it clear that the location parameter is required for
every weather forecast request. In such a case, you could ask the following question to the LLM:
What's the weather today?
It would most probably reply something like this:
Could you tell me your location…
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 308
Complete your answer:
Brussels
Then, it will be capable of crafting the function call that needs to be made in order to obtain the
answer:
get_weather({"location":"Brussels"})
It’s worth mentioning that the LLM never directly executes a function itself. Instead, it returns a
structured response indicating which function should be called and with what parameters. In the
preceding example, you might have noticed that the LLM performed NER (which we discussed
earlier) and captured the Brussels entity to pass it to the function. It is then up to your applica -
tion code to evaluate this response, perform the actual function call, and feed the result back to
the LLM to complete the interaction.
TAG is nothing more than that. Today, there are many tools that specialize in specific tasks such
as converting natural language into SQL queries, and so on. Frameworks such as Semantic Ker -
nel help abstract the injection of the function signature. For example, a function declaration in
Semantic Kernel may look like this:
var plugin = kernel.ImportPluginFromObject(new MyTools(), "MyTools");
public class MyTools {
[KernelFunction]
public async Task< string > GetWeather (string location) => ...
}
It instructs Semantic Kernel to inject the corresponding function signature into the prompt sent
to the LLM, making the model aware of the function’s availability. This code is more maintain -
able than directly injecting the function signature but ultimately ends up with the same result.
You can equip your AI solution with as many tools as needed, but this quickly introduces chal -
lenges that go beyond AI itself—particularly around scalability and security.
For example, an AI application may have to interact with a variety of services, as shown in Figure

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 309
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 309
Figure 8.10 – TAG application calling many different tools
Each target system might require different authentication mechanisms and might be based on
different protocols. This can be challenging at scale.
Additionally, from a security point of view, how do you ensure that a user interacting with a chat
interface has the appropriate permissions to perform actions A or B? This concern also applies to
RAG and its variants. If your RAG solution ingests an entire SharePoint repository—where access to
documents is typically security-trimmed—how can you guarantee that the user asking a question
is actually authorized to receive the answer? How do you ensure that your RAG implementation
respects those same access controls? The more you build and scale AI solutions, the more often
you’ll encounter these types of real-world constraints.
In conclusion, while TAG brings greater capabilities to any AI solution, it lacks a standard way to
interact with remote systems. A partial answer to this is Model Context Protocol (MCP), which
we will discuss in the next section.
Model context protocol
As of June 2025, MCP remains an emerging pattern and is highly subject to change in the future,
but the philosophy behind it should remain the same.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 310
As noted in the previous section, implementing the TAG pattern at scale can be challenging, since
an AI application may need to interface with numerous services, each with its own quirks. This
complexity becomes difficult to manage.
MCP partially addresses this challenge by defining a standardized way to describe features and
tools. Each tool can implement its own MCP server, while each consuming service maintains
its own set of MCP clients. These clients and servers communicate using a common protocol,
ensuring consistent interaction patterns.
At this stage, the relationship between each client and server is one to one. The MCP server acts
as an abstraction layer over the underlying remote service—such as a database or an API—and
encapsulates the logic required to interact with that service.
The application remains the orchestrator between the LLM and its set of MCP resources. However,
it no longer needs to implement custom, ad hoc interactions for each individual service and can in -
stead rely on MCP to standardize those interactions. Figure 8.11 provides a high-level view of MCP:
Figure 8.11 – High-level view of an MCP-enabled application

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 311
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 311
In Figure 8.11, the application uses its various MCP clients to retrieve metadata about the tools
and resources exposed by their corresponding MCP servers. At this stage of MCP adoption, most
AI solutions host both MCP clients and servers themselves. This approach is primarily driven by
security concerns, as full trust in MCP—particularly from a security standpoint—has not yet
been established.
Typically, service owners develop the MCP server and distribute it as a container image or a
package that can be integrated with different AI solutions.
An MCP server will typically expose at least the following operations:
@server.list_tools()
@server.list_prompts()
@server.call_tool()
@server.get_prompt()
These operations allow clients to fetch information and call the tools exposed by the server.
While running a local MCP server is appropriate for accessing local resources, it becomes less
suitable for interacting with remote resources exposed by remote services.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 312
The concept of a remote MCP server exists in the MCP specification but is not yet mainstream
due to the lack of security. However, in the Azure ecosystem, APIM positions itself as a possible
solution for remote MCP servers, as shown in Figure 8.12.
Figure 8.12 – Using APIM as a remote MCP server
APIM can automatically generate the MCP server layer for any API already published to a given
APIM instance. In addition, APIM policies can be used to enforce security measures such as JWT to -
ken validation and throttling—ensuring that the underlying remote systems are securely exposed.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 313
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 313
APIM can also act as a proxy for existing remote MCP servers, helping to standardize how such
servers are exposed and consumed across different environments. When integrated with Applica -
tion Insights, it provides centralized logging and monitoring of all MCP client/server interactions.
While the MCP ecosystem is still evolving, it’s expected that remote MCP servers will become the
standard, with local MCP servers being limited to accessing strictly local resources.
Next, let’s explore agentic AI.
Agentic AI
Agentic AI goes beyond being a simple design pattern—it encompasses any autonomous AI system
capable of making decisions and performing tasks without human intervention. For instance, an
agent could independently book a hotel room by evaluating factors such as price, comfort, and
availability. A key characteristic of agentic AI is the ability of agents to tackle complex tasks, which
requires them to reason and formulate a plan to achieve the desired outcome.
An example of a complex task could be the autonomous planning of a technical intervention
of a malfunctioning fridge in a retail store (see the smart fridge monitoring in retail stores use
case in Chapter 7), detected by a monitoring system. The agent would be triggered by the alert.
It should be able to find the most appropriate technician, check availability, and so on. It would
take multiple steps and important coordination to make this possible.
However, to achieve this, the agent would most probably leverage a few of the patterns we have
learned about so far, such as RAG (knowledge), persist state, TAG (tooling), and MCP (context
and tooling), to augment the agent’s capabilities. An agent might rely on other agents to make a
decision. This is called multi-agent orchestration. The context, tooling, reasoning, and knowledge
can be added using low-code or pro-code solutions.
If you’re just getting started with agentic AI, the Copilot Studio portal is an excellent entry point.
It offers a low-code approach that makes it easier to grasp the principles behind agentic AI and
achieve meaningful results without the complexity of building everything from scratch.
Copilot Studio integrates seamlessly with the broader Microsoft ecosystem, enabling you to
build event-driven agents that can respond to specific triggers—such as receiving an email or
the creation of a SharePoint document. You can also schedule agent activities using the recurrence
trigger type, allowing agents to run at predefined intervals.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 314
For code-based solutions, Semantic Kernel is Microsoft’s open source, enterprise-ready framework
designed to orchestrate and manage both single- and multi-agent workflows. In contrast, Auto -
Gen, developed by Microsoft Research, explores more advanced and experimental scenarios but

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 313
chunks.content:
is still evolving and subject to change. For building robust enterprise-grade solutions, Semantic
Kernel is the recommended choice.
Semantic Kernel makes it easy to establish communication between agents thanks to different
orchestration mechanisms, as illustrated in Figure 8.13.
Figure 8.13 – Orchestration types in Semantic Kernel
The following is an explanation of these orchestration types:
• Sequential orchestration: Agents pass tasks along a pipeline. This is typically required
for multi-stage reasoning.
• Group chat: Agents are part of a group and are able to communicate with each other until
the termination state, configured by a termination strategy, is reached.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 315
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 315
• Concurrent orchestration: Multiple agents work on the same task in parallel.
• Handoff orchestration: Agents can transfer control to other agents in the pipeline if needed.
All agents know each other.
• Magentic orchestration: This orchestration model is inherited from AutoGen’s Magen -
tic-One and is aimed at solving complex business tasks by appointing a central lead agent
that coordinates workflow activities. Other agents do not know each other.
Semantic Kernel is available for .NET, Java, and Python. It’s worth exploring Semantic Kernel’s
GitHub repo: https://github.com/microsoft/semantic-kernel.
The world of agentic AI involves many moving parts, but Dapr—which we explored in Chapter 5,
Working with Other Container Services —also offers native support for agents. Dapr Agents lever -
ages core Dapr building blocks such as service-to-service invocation, pub/sub messaging, state
management, durable workflows, and the actor model to create both stateless and stateful agents.
If you’re already using Dapr to develop distributed applications, its built-in support for agentic
AI is certainly worth exploring. Supported patterns and orchestration types are documented in
this GitHub repo: https://github.com/dapr/dapr-agents.
In essence, that is all we could safely say about the core principles of agentic AI at this stage. We
prefer not to dive too much into technical details as frameworks and tools keep changing on a
weekly basis.
Next, let’s explore the AI gateway feature of APIM, which can play a key role in whatever AI solu -
tion you’re trying to build.
AI gateway through APIM
As discussed earlier, in the Model context protocol section, APIM has already embraced the MCP
model by positioning itself as a remote MCP server for APIs published on APIM, or as a proxy to
other MCP servers. However, its involvement in the GenAI space goes even further.
The extra capabilities are part of the API gateway referred to as the AI gateway, but this is the
same gateway as for non-AI solutions.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 316
Figure 8.14 shows a subset of capabilities made available by APIM’s AI gateway:
Figure 8.14 – A few AI gateway capabilities
Here is a detailed explanation of each pattern:
• Load balancing: This pattern leverages APIM’s backend pool feature by registering mul -
tiple LLMs as backends of the pool. Additionally, a custom retry policy can be used in
case of transient failures of one of the backends or in case of throttling from the LLM.
The load-balancing algorithm defaults to round-robin but can be influenced by setting
priority and weight-based routing.
• Model routing: At first glance, this pattern might resemble the load-balancing one, but it
fulfills a completely different need. In essence, this pattern consists of routing the request

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 315
chunks.content:
to the appropriate model (different model versions, such as GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, etc.) based
on request parameters.
• Semantic caching: This pattern enables caching of LLM responses in an external store
such as Redis, allowing subsequent requests to check the cache for similar prompts before
querying the LLM again.
• Rate limiting: This pattern allows enforcing rate-limiting policies prior to forwarding
traffic to the LLMs. This is a good protection against LLMs’ abusive usage.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 317
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 317
• Message storing: This pattern leverages the log-to-eventhub policy to send all messages
to Event Hubs. From there on, you can stream those messages with Stream Analytics or
other services to get these messages landing in an operational or analytical data store.
• Response streaming: This pattern ensures that SSE headers are added to the response
when needed.
It’s worth noting that these patterns can be combined, as most are not mutually exclusive.
While additional patterns exist, this provides a solid foundation to begin with. The key takeaway
about the AI gateway is that it shields the client from temporary LLM outages, throttling, and
even changes in the underlying model. APIM serves as a bridge between the client and the target
LLMs, and it can also handle authentication on their behalf—minimizing direct exposure of the
LLMs themselves.
Now, let’s explore a use case.
Use case – AI-driven rule management for tax data
processing
Here is the scenario and first analysis:
Contoso is a well-established company operating in the tax domain. Their core business in -
volves receiving tax transaction files from customers that must undergo validation, cleansing,
and compliance checks before being submitted to local tax authorities. The data transformation
and compliance rules are highly complex and differ significantly across countries.
Given the high volume of data and the need for low-latency processing, Contoso’s data platform
is built on Azure Databricks, which provides the scalability and performance required for large-
scale data transformation workloads. The heavy-lifting data transformation process is done by
Databricks, but the business performs the final review prior to submitting the resulting files to
the authorities.
However, because regulations keep changing, Contoso would like to gain greater agility and aims
to empower business users to define these transformation and validation rules using natural
language. They currently have a rule engine, but it lacks flexibility and is not intuitive enough. By
leveraging AI, the organization seeks to translate these natural language inputs into executable
rules that can be integrated back into their underlying data platform.
Before these AI-generated rules are injected into production pipelines, Contoso would like to sim -
ulate their application against representative data samples to verify correctness and effectiveness.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 318
Let’s first extract the keywords in this scenario that demand our focus:
• Define data transformation rules using natural language: Business users would like
to define rules by simply expressing them in natural language. This means that we must
foresee an NLP-friendly AI model to help us.
• Inline validation and injection of the generated rules back into the Azure Databricks

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 317
chunks.content:
data platform: Databricks performs the heavy-lifting data transformation using broader
rulesets that apply to specific countries. We must be able to enrich those rulesets through
a feedback loop mechanism.
After some investigation and prompt engineering techniques, we conclude that LLMs are not that
good at checking and adjusting data by themselves, especially when dealing with numbers of all
types (double, integer, and so on) and calculations. Instead, we realize that we could leverage
LLMs to generate PySpark code snippets that implement the rules defined by end users, which
we could reinject into Databricks. We go to the drawing board and end up with the high-level
view shown in Figure 8.15, discussed in the next section.
Diagrams
Figure 8.15 illustrates a possible architecture for this use case.
Figure 8.15 – Possible architecture for the use case

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 319
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 319
Users interact with a user interface to monitor ongoing operations and perform pre- and post-Da -
tabricks checks, along with optional additional data transformations. The interface may include
a chat window, allowing users to request the application of new transformation rules. These re -
quests are sent from the browser to a Backend for Frontend (BFF), if used, which then forwards
them to the chat API. The chat API communicates with the LLM via the AI gateway to generate
the corresponding PySpark code.
Effective prompt engineering is essential to ensure that the LLM returns only the relevant code
snippet. Once received, the generated code can be displayed to the user, who may choose to ex -
ecute an in-cluster test against a sample dataset and review the output.
If the user approves the result, the code can be committed to a Git repository—triggering an
Azure DevOps pipeline (or an equivalent CI/CD tool) to run a Databricks job on a larger dataset.
This use case demonstrates the value of leveraging code generation rather than relying on the
LLM to analyze the data directly. A more effective approach is to express the desired rules and
have the LLM generate the corresponding code to implement them.
Let’s now summarize what we have learned in the chapter.
Summary
This chapter has shown that while GenAI is transforming how we build intelligent applications,
traditional AI remains highly relevant for structured, cost-effective, and high-precision tasks.
We explored how Azure supports both paradigms through services such as Azure ML, AI Vision,
and AI Language, and how foundational NLP techniques such as tokenization, POS tagging, and
entity recognition still underpin many modern solutions.
We examined the growing role of embeddings and vector search in GenAI scenarios, comparing
Azure’s options and trade-offs for storing and querying vector data. Key architectural patterns,
such as RAG, CAG, and TAG, were discussed, each addressing different constraints around data
access, performance, and actionability. MCP was introduced as an emerging solution to stan -
dardize interactions between AI agents and external tools, helping reduce complexity at scale.
Agentic AI was explored as the natural evolution of these patterns, combining reasoning, planning,
and orchestration to tackle complex tasks autonomously. Frameworks such as Semantic Kernel,
Dapr, and tools such as Copilot Studio illustrate how both pro-code and low-code solutions can
support this shift. Finally, the AI gateway capabilities of APIM were highlighted as essential for
building scalable, secure, and resilient AI architectures.
Artificial Intelligence Architecture 320
The chapter closed with a practical use case that illustrated how LLMs can generate executable
PySpark code from natural language inputs, enabling a feedback loop between business users

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 319
chunks.content:
and data pipelines. Rather than relying on LLMs to interpret data directly, empowering them to
generate code offers a more reliable, testable, and maintainable path forward.
In the next chapter, we will turn our focus to security architecture. Chapter 9 will guide you through
the principles, patterns, and native Azure capabilities you can use to build secure-by-design
architectures that remain resilient against evolving threats.

Security Architecture
Security is a foundational pillar of any cloud architecture, and in Azure, it encompasses a broad
set of capabilities and shared responsibilities across identity, data, infrastructure, and operational
practices. In this chapter, we explore the key aspects of securing solutions on Azure, focusing
on Identity and Access Management (IDAM) through Entra ID and modern authentication
protocols; data security through encryption, classification, and governance; and Cloud Security
Posture Management (CSPM), as well as Cloud Workload Protection Platforms (CWPPs), to
ensure continuous compliance and threat visibility.
We will also cover DevSecOps practices, including Static Application Security Testing (SAST) and
Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST), and the integration of security controls in CI/CD
pipelines. Operational Security (SecOps) is addressed through the use of Security Information
Event Management (SIEM) and Security Orchestration Automation and Response (SOAR)
tools such as Microsoft Sentinel and Defender for Cloud.
More specifically, we’ll look at the following topics:
• Introducing cloud-native security and cloud-native security principles
• Laying the foundations for cloud security
• Zooming in on data security
• Zooming in on identity
• Zooming in on CSPM
• Zooming in on CWPPs
• Zooming in on DevSecOps
• Zooming in on SecOps
• Zooming in on appliances and CASB solutions
Security Architecture 322
While the network remains a critical security layer, it has already been covered in detail in Chap -
ter 3, Infrastructure Design, and Chapter 4, Working with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). Therefore,
in this chapter, we’ll assume that you are routing and filtering traffic appropriately and using
Private Link all the way.
The availability aspect of the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA) triad was thor -
oughly addressed in Chapter 3, where we discussed the various options, such as availability zones,
geo-replication, and backup/restore capabilities. This chapter will instead focus primarily on
confidentiality and integrity, which are just as essential in building secure cloud-native applications.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 319
chunks.content:
Let us now explore the technical requirements.
Technical requirements
There are no technical requirements for this chapter. The maps and diagrams are available at
https://github.com/PacktPublishing/The-Azure-Cloud-Native-Architecture-Mapbook-
Second-Edition/tree/main/Chapter09.
Introducing cloud-native security
As we’ve seen in the previous chapters, the cloud offers significant advantages in accelerating
solution development and deployment while optimizing costs. However, these benefits can only
be fully realized if we also modernize how we approach security. Cloud-native security embraces
the shift-left principle, which emphasizes incorporating security earlier in the asset life cycle.
Addressing security from the outset helps avoid late-stage issues and deployment delays. That
said, implementing this approach is often more challenging than it sounds.
In many cases, developers—particularly early adopters—and infrastructure teams have adopt -
ed modern practices such as infrastructure as code, while security teams remain entrenched in
traditional, reactive, and waterfall-driven processes. It’s not uncommon for firewall rule changes
to take days to be approved and implemented, which stands in stark contrast to the shift-left
philosophy and undermines the progress made by other teams.
With the right tools and technologies, security has become declarative. As discussed in Chapter 3,
Infrastructure Design, and Chapter 4, Working with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), CI/CD pipelines
enable organizations to provision both code and infrastructure consistently. The same automa -
tion can be extended to security, especially in cloud-native platforms such as Kubernetes, where
elements such as layer 4 (transport) and layer 7 (application) policies are defined as code and
automated.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 323
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 323
However, cloud-native security is not just about tools and technology—it requires a cultural shift.
Organizations must rethink their structure and embrace a new mindset, which can be difficult in
environments with deep-rooted legacy practices. Regardless of your industry or regulatory land -
scape, there are always opportunities to improve automation and streamline security processes.
Regulations typically define what must be achieved, not how to achieve it. Many organizations
in the insurance and financial industries entirely rely on manual processes and lengthy approval
steps before opening a flow between a source and a target. While this is understandable, it dra -
matically impacts the time to market and agility.
In a cloud-native model, security architects must create value by enabling automation and en -
suring that security processes do not hinder progress. They should serve as enablers —educating
other teams on security’s importance, offering practical solutions, and supporting risk-based
decisions. They must assess risks objectively and allow the business to determine which residual
risks are acceptable. They should contribute to architectural patterns that encompass the security
dimension so as to quicken approval processes.
This mindset shift is particularly difficult in risk-averse sectors such as banking, where cautious -
ness is ingrained. The degree to which an organization can evolve from traditional to cloud-na -
tive security practices often depends on its inherent culture. But one thing is clear: while cloud
technologies can deliver on promises of cost efficiency, speed, resilience, and scalability, these
outcomes are unreachable without a fundamental change in security practices. Security is a core
pillar of cloud success—or failure.
From a technical standpoint, there has also been a significant shift toward identity as the primary
layer of defense rather than the network, although Microsoft has closed many gaps in terms of
network capabilities over recent years. However, network-based security still tends to be more
complex, costly, and rigid. Unfortunately, many traditional security architects continue to rely
heavily on perimeter-focused strategies (the DMZ mindset), often overlooking identity-based
security.
In this chapter, we will offer guidance on adopting a cloud-native security posture and highlight
traditional approaches that may hinder your cloud journey. Keep in mind that your ability to
succeed in the cloud is closely tied to your ability to modernize your security practices.
Let’s explore some key guidelines to help establish the right mindset and lay strong foundations
for your cloud security journey.
Security Architecture 324
Laying the foundations for cloud security
After years of working extensively with Azure, I’ve observed a recurring pattern across many

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 323
chunks.content:
organizations: security teams often replicate their on-premises security stack in the cloud with -
out adaptation. Familiar names such as F5, Netskope, Palo Alto firewalls, Splunk, QRadar, and
CyberArk frequently make their way into cloud environments by default. While these established
tools are not inherently problematic, they often introduce additional complexity and are adopted
without evaluating Microsoft-native alternatives.
The rationale is usually the same: the desire for a unified single pane of glass across environments,
or statements such as: “ Palo Alto firewalls are better than Azure Firewall.” While it is true that niche
products are often richer than Azure alternatives, too often, decisions are driven by product famil -
iarity and internal expertise rather than actual business, regulatory, or technical requirements. A
key contributor to this trend is the lack of Azure/Microsoft-specific expertise within security teams.
How many certified Azure security professionals can you typically find in a CISO organization?
Think about your own organization and you will be surprised by the number. It’s often close to zero.
The single-pane-of-glass argument is very valid and used to justify relying on legacy or third-party
security tools across environments. However, it’s important to recognize that many Azure-native
services are now designed to work beyond Azure, supporting hybrid and multi-cloud scenarios as
well. Microsoft has gradually renamed several services to emphasize that they are no longer lim -
ited to Azure. As for concerns about feature gaps between Azure-native products and third-party
solutions, Microsoft has consistently shown a strong pace of innovation, rapidly closing gaps,
and introducing new capabilities. Once a native service gains traction, feature parity with more
established competitors is often reached sooner than expected.
The added complexity of using non-native products stems from the operational overhead they
introduce. When relying on third-party tools, organizations are fully responsible for ensuring
high availability, scalability, and disaster recovery—capabilities that are typically built into Azure
services natively and managed by Microsoft. Additionally, native solutions offer tighter and bet -
ter integration, simplified management, and higher resilience, allowing teams to focus more on
outcomes rather than infrastructure.
Here are a few principles that might help trigger the correct behavior when designing security
solutions in Azure and Kubernetes:

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 325
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 325
• Know the risk appetite of your organization: Security decisions should primarily be
guided by the organization’s risk appetite and business drivers. There is no one-size-fits-
all approach—what works for a bank with limited risk tolerance will differ significantly
from a digital-native company offering entertainment services.
• Best of suite over best of breed: Whatever security challenge you’re addressing, always
start by evaluating the native Azure offering and how well it integrates with the broad -
er Azure ecosystem. For example, most Azure services are designed to work seamlessly
with Azure Key Vault for managing secrets, certificates, and encryption keys. Choosing
a third-party vault solution could introduce friction or limit this native integration. Fur -
thermore, all Azure services support full automation through infrastructure as code. If
you opt for custom or third-party solutions, you must ensure they align with these auto -
mation capabilities and evaluate how they integrate with the Azure ecosystem, to avoid
disrupting your cloud experience. Following this principle is even more important in
container orchestration platforms.
• Assess trust in Microsoft and clearly identify your responsibilities: The cloud operates
on a shared responsibility model, which inherently means relinquishing full control over
certain aspects of the infrastructure. While this may seem straightforward, many security
teams struggle to fully embrace this reality. Rather than attempting to uncover the inner
workings of multi-tenant service offerings, organizations should focus on clearly under -
standing and addressing their own areas of responsibility within the model. This shift in
mindset is essential for building an effective and sustainable cloud security posture. The
other aspects that you do not control should be covered by SLAs and Microsoft’s liability
with regard to security breaches that may affect your organization. It is then up to your
legal department to evaluate this part.
• Conduct thorough risk assessments and document residual risks: Many security teams
still lack robust risk assessment practices. A common example is the handling of container
image vulnerabilities. It’s not unusual to see blanket policies—such as zero high vulner -
abilities —that block deployments without evaluating the actual risk or context. This
rigid approach often leads to unnecessary friction and delays. A more effective strategy
involves assessing whether identified vulnerabilities are exploitable within your specific
environment, considering other mitigating controls already in place. In some cases, it may
be entirely acceptable to deploy containers with high-severity vulnerabilities if they pose
no real threat under current conditions. This observation applies to everything you do in

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 325
chunks.content:
Azure, not just containers.
Security Architecture 326
• Adapting CISO practices to cloud-native realities: Shift left and DevSecOps are far more
than industry buzzwords—they are critical enablers for adopting cloud-native practic -
es and unlocking the full potential of the cloud. However, their effectiveness is limited
if CISO-led security processes are not reimagined to align with the realities of modern,
inherently disruptive IT environments. In a world where everything is defined as code,
developers and infrastructure engineers can now implement network and service mesh
policies directly. While these actions must remain under the CISO’s oversight, they are
incompatible with traditional ticket-based workflows. This highlights the urgent need
for the CISO function to evolve and embrace new operational models that support agility
without compromising compliance.
• Choose appropriate compliance frameworks: When selecting a security framework,
choose one that aligns well with cloud environments and with local regulatory obligations.
For instance, ISO/IEC 27001:2013 does not fully account for the shared responsibility
model, as it includes controls related to physical infrastructure—something cloud cus -
tomers typically cannot influence. If you choose ISO, consider adopting the 2022 revision,
which better reflects modern IT realities. Alternatively, frameworks such as CIS Controls
v8.1 offer more actionable guidance for assessing cloud-specific hardening and SecOps.
Remember, frameworks are not mutually exclusive—you can combine them to cover
different aspects of your security posture. Make sure to stay away from any in-house
compliance frameworks as they will likely not be relevant at all for a cloud environment.
This list of fundamental principles is not exhaustive, and the degree to which they should be
applied will depend on the specific Azure and Kubernetes footprint you intend to establish in the
cloud, and on your risk appetite. Let’s now explore the Security Architecture Map.

duties of an Azure security architect:
