Security Architecture 328
• Data Security: In this section, we’ll explore the different encryption mechanisms, as well
as key stores such as Azure Key Vault and Hardware Security Module (HSM) options.
We’ll also talk about Microsoft Purview, which has become the data governance Swiss
Army knife.
• Identity: In this section, we’ll explore how Entra ID enables strong identity security
through Conditional Access Policies (CAPs) and Privileged Identity Management (PIM),
as well as how to combine different mechanisms to achieve a tier 0/red tenant architec -
ture, an emerging pattern. We will also explore the OIDC and OAuth protocols, which
are paramount in the cloud.
• CSPM: This section provides an overview of Azure’s CSPM capabilities, focusing on how
tools such as Microsoft Defender for Cloud (foundational) help continuously assess, mon -
itor, and improve the security posture of your Azure environment by identifying miscon -
figurations, enforcing best practices, and ensuring compliance with regulatory standards.
• CWPP: This section highlights how Defender can be used to protect running workloads.
• SecOps: This section introduces Azure’s SIEM and SOAR capabilities through Microsoft
Sentinel, highlighting how it enables centralized threat detection, investigation, and re -
sponse. It covers how automation and orchestration help reduce response times, improve
incident handling, and enhance overall security operations efficiency.
• DevSecOps: This section explores the integration of security into the development life
cycle through DevSecOps practices. It highlights which technologies and services are
used to embed security checks, policy enforcement, and compliance validation into CI/
CD pipelines.
• Appliances and CASB: This section explores a few common concerns, such as TLS inspec -
tion, firewalls, and Web Application Firewalls (WAFs), as well as introducing the Cloud
Access Security Broker (CASB) concept.
As stated in the introduction, the CIA triad is a foundational model in information security. Since
we previously explored the availability dimension in detail in Chapter 3, Infrastructure Design, we
will shift our focus to the remaining pillars: integrity and confidentiality.
Let’s see how to ensure confidentiality and integrity in the next section.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 327
chunks.content:
Zooming in on data security
In this section, we will examine the various types of encryption and the options available for
storing encryption keys. We will also cover data governance and data-specific features that help
protect against integrity loss. Figure 9.2 illustrates the different data security features:

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 329
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 329
Figure 9.2 – Data security features
Understanding encryption mechanisms and capabilities
Before diving into the specific details, let’s first review the different encryption types and Azure-re -
lated capabilities:
• Encryption at rest: This type of encryption safeguards data at rest (stored) by ensuring it
remains unreadable if the storage device is stolen or accessed with malicious intent. Most
Azure services let you Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) or, by default, use Microsoft-managed
keys to ensure data at rest is always encrypted. An additional possibility is Host Your
Own Key (HYOK), which means that you generate the keys and store them in hardware
that you control. Be aware that this option is mostly compatible with Infrastructure as a Service.
• Encryption in transit: This type of encryption protects data in motion. For example, when
accessing https://portal.azure.com using a web browser, the client initiates a TLS
connection with the Azure server. During this process, the client verifies the legitimacy
of the server by validating its certificate, and both sides perform a key exchange to derive
a shared symmetric encryption key. This key is then used to encrypt all subsequent data
transmitted between the client and server.
Security Architecture 330
Asymmetric cryptography is used during the handshake to authenticate the server and
secure the key exchange process. Simply put, this type of encryption ensures that someone
sniffing the network would only see encrypted data and not clear text. As for encryption
at rest, Azure services default to Microsoft-managed certificates, but most services let
you Bring Your Own Certificate (BYOC). When using BYOC, you typically store them in
Azure Key Vault and integrate Azure services with Key Vault to let them pull the certificate.
You may Host Your Own Certificate (HYOC) by storing private keys in hardware that you
control. Be aware that this is absolutely not compatible with Azure PaaS services.
• Encryption in use: This type of encryption protects in-memory data. As with the previous
example, without encryption in use, any administrator or system process of a machine
might perform memory inspection and see data in clear text. In Azure, encryption in use
is offered through the broader confidential computing concept.
Encryption at rest and in transit in Azure rely by default on Microsoft-managed keys. This is by far
the easiest way to leverage Azure services. Many companies rely on these defaults and only bring
their own certificates for internet-facing web apps and APIs. From that perspective, it’s worth
noting that Azure Key Vault has built-in integration mechanisms with well-known Certificate
Authorities (CAs), such as GlobalSign and DigiCert, including automatic certificate renewal.
However, many other companies have regulatory obligations to store encryption keys in HSMs or

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 329
chunks.content:
do not feel comfortable with the US Patriot Act, allowing the National Security Agency (NSA) to
request data from any US company, wherever the data is stored, whether on national territory or
anywhere else. Of course, companies such as Microsoft and Amazon resist these legal obligations,
but the risk is definitely not null. It is worth mentioning that this statement does not apply to
Azure China, since Microsoft doesn’t operate those data centers.
For this very reason, many organizations turn to customer-managed keys to strengthen their
data protection. This naturally raises the question: where should these keys be stored? How can
we be safe against the previously mentioned threats?
The safest approach to mitigate all the risks linked to potential third-party interference is HYOK,
where encryption keys never leave your on-premises infrastructure. Unfortunately, this approach
is compatible with a very limited number of services, such as Microsoft 365. Additionally, keeping
keys on-premises introduces latency and can undermine resilience by creating a tight dependen -
cy between the cloud and your on-premises infrastructure—an approach that is far from ideal.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 331
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 331
HYOK aside, Azure comes with many different options to store your keys. The full list, along with
the drivers that should help you choose the best option for your use case, is available here: https://
learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/key-management-choose.
There are a few factors to consider before choosing an option:
• Service model: What service model are you primarily using—IaaS, PaaS, CaaS, or FaaS?
This question alone can rule out several options. For instance, Azure Dedicated HSM
doesn’t natively integrate with any Azure PaaS services, making it incompatible with that
model. On the other hand, a few PaaS services support Azure Managed HSM, and nearly
all of them are compatible with Azure Key Vault.
• Regulatory requirements: Regulatory requirements are often tied to Federal Information
Processing Standards (FIPS) levels. Select the option that aligns most closely with your
compliance obligations.
• Root of trust control and key sovereignty: Choose any of the compatible options if you
require full control over your encryption keys and want to ensure that Microsoft has no
access to them.
Table 9.1 describes a few scenarios to help you choose:
Scenario Best option
You are not a regulated industry Azure Key Vault Standard or Premium
You are a regulated industry and you plan to
use mostly PaaS services
Azure Key Vault Premium
You are a regulated industry and key
sovereignty is critical, and you plan to use
mostly PaaS services
Managed HSM
You plan to use IaaS (self-hosted databases,
etc.) as the main service model
Any HSM option, including HYOK (with the
drawbacks highlighted earlier)
You want full control over the HSM Dedicated HSM or HYOK
Table 9.1 – Choosing a key store
Be aware that with Azure Dedicated HSM, you are fully responsible for all aspects of management,
including firmware upgrades, patching, and ensuring high availability and disaster recovery.
For instance, achieving zone redundancy requires you to provision two separate Dedicated HSM
instances and deploy them in different availability zones. Additionally, you must also foresee all
integrations yourself using the Luna client or other compatible libraries.
Security Architecture 332
Now, let’s dive a bit deeper into the underlying encryption mechanisms.
Understanding data encryption keys and key encryption keys
Something important to grasp is the role of the Data Encryption Key (DEK) and Key Encryp -
tion Key (KEK). When you BYOK, you actually bring your own KEK. This KEK never leaves the
boundaries of the HSM. Asymmetric encryption is used to encrypt the DEK through key wrap
and unwrap operations. The encrypted DEK is stored on the server side in the Azure service, but
the unencrypted symmetric key lives in memory. This means that the actual encryption key used

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 331
chunks.content:
to encrypt the data is in fact available in the memory of the servers used by the service. One way
to protect in-memory information is to rely on encryption in use (discussed in the next section),
which translates to confidential computing in Azure. While you can use confidential computing
for virtual machines and container solutions such as AKS, you do not control this for PaaS services.
One way to retain control over the DEKs is through client-side encryption, where data is encrypt -
ed before being stored in the cloud. However, this approach can be cumbersome, can introduce
performance overhead, and does not play well with cloud-only workloads.
Introducing encryption in use
Data-in-use encryption protects against in-memory attacks such as memory dumps, compro -
mised processes, and memory scraping. Without such encryption, sensitive data in memory may
be exposed in plaintext.
The goal is to encrypt in-memory data and process it inside secure enclaves, which are protected
environments that restrict access to authorized code. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs),
such as Intel SGX and AMD SEV, enable these enclaves using hardware-based security features.
Confidential computing is a broader paradigm that encompasses TEEs and other technologies to
protect data while it is in use—complementing encryption at rest and in transit. Azure includes
several services that are associated with confidential computing. You can visit this link to get
an exhaustive list: https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/solutions/confidential-compute.
Let’s now look at different ways to maintain data integrity.
Preserving data integrity
Data access can be controlled using Azure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). All Azure services—
whether data-centric or not—generate activity logs that capture control plane operations. These
logs can be ingested by Azure Sentinel or any other SIEM solution for comprehensive monitoring.
For data plane activities, certain services, such as Azure SQL, provide dedicated audit logs.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 333
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 333
To safeguard against accidental deletions or modifications, Azure offers features such as soft delete,
purge protection, and versioning for some services. Cosmos DB includes a change feed mechanism
that tracks operations performed on data. Additionally, Azure SQL and Synapse support dynamic
data masking, allowing sensitive information to be obfuscated at runtime. Additionally, backup
solutions such as a Backup vault allow us to take immutable backups.
In summary, it’s essential to verify which features are supported by the data services you intend
to use and to enable data protection-specific features.
Next, let’s talk about data governance.
Ensuring proper data governance
Selecting the appropriate encryption model and mitigating possible integrity issues is an import -
ant part of governance, but it’s only one piece of the puzzle. Equally critical is implementing a
robust data classification framework to differentiate between general data, sensitive information,
and intellectual property. This classification helps determine the level of protection required
and guides encryption, access control, and auditing policies accordingly. Microsoft Purview has
evolved into a unified service that delivers a consolidated experience for data governance. While
it is deeply integrated with Microsoft 365, especially in the areas of information protection and
data loss prevention, our focus here will be limited to its Azure-specific capabilities and how
Purview can help with data governance within the Azure ecosystem.
The Microsoft Purview Data Map is one of the core components to integrate Azure data services
with Microsoft Purview. For the Data Map to show up in the Purview portal (https://purview.
microsoft.com/), you must have a Purview account created in Azure.
Once you have a Purview account in Azure, the Data Map component will be available in the
Purview portal. From there, you can organize a hierarchy of collections and subcollections to deal
with the various data sources in an organized way, as shown in Figure 9.3.
Figure 9.3 – Organizing Data Map collections and subcollections
Security Architecture 334
All the collections are bound to a domain, and multiple domains can be created.
We can assign permissions at each level, which helps delegate data management operations to
different teams. Figure 9.3 illustrates a sample hierarchy based on resource types, but you could
also structure it by location or any other attribute relevant to your organization.
Using the Data Map, you can scan Azure data sources, allowing Microsoft Purview to automat -
ically discover and classify sensitive data. This provides comprehensive visibility across your
data landscape.
We can connect the Data Map to a variety of data sources, such as Blob Storage, Data Lake, Cosmos

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 333
chunks.content:
DB, Azure SQL, Data Explorer, Databricks, and Synapse. It also has connectors for Fabric and AWS.
Figure 9.4 shows how we can connect the Data Map to Azure Blob Storage:
Figure 9.4 – Data Map connected to Azure Blob Storage
Figure 9.4 illustrates a storage account that has public access disabled. Microsoft Purview connects
to it using managed private endpoints. As a best practice, it is recommended to use user-assigned
managed identities to access target data sources. This approach supports the principle of least
privilege by ensuring each identity is granted only the specific permissions needed on the cor -
responding data source.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 335
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 335
With this setup in place, we performed a scan on our storage account, which contained random
PDF invoices. As shown in Figure 9.5, Purview successfully identified sensitive financial informa -
tion, including bank account numbers, through its automated classification capabilities.
Figure 9.5 – Automatic classification
We used the default scanning ruleset for a storage account, but we can create our own rulesets.
This example shows how useful Purview can be to keep control over data stored in Azure. Purview
shines even more with well-structured data, such as relational databases.
This concludes our section on data security. Now, let’s turn our attention to identity—the primary
security layer in the cloud.
Security Architecture 336
Zooming in on identity
The identity landscape in Azure is very broad. Figure 9.6 depicts its most important parts:
Figure 9.6 – Identity landscape
Let’s now dive into specific sections, starting with IDAM and CIAM.
Introducing the main solutions used for IDAM and CIAM
Entra ID serves as the foundation for IDAM across the Microsoft ecosystem. Every Azure subscrip -
tion is associated with an Entra ID instance, referred to as a tenant. Corporate users, including
employees and collaborators, have identities in Entra ID to carry out their daily tasks. In many
organizations, an on-premises Active Directory remains in use and is synchronized with Entra ID
via Entra Connect. While federating Entra ID with Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS)
was once common, this approach is now discouraged due to the increasing centrality of Entra ID
over the past decade. AD FS was mostly used to establish identity federation with partners and
integrate with on-premises, but this has now shifted to Entra ID. Today, Entra ID stands as the
core component of any IDAM strategy.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 337
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 337
In the realm of Customer Identity and Access Management (CIAM), Entra ID is often used to
provide external or customer access to Microsoft 365 through B2B guest invitations, also known
as B2B collaboration, and to allow external partners/customers to access organizational assets
through federation. However, Microsoft positions Entra External ID, formerly Azure B2C, as its
dedicated CIAM solution, designed from the ground up to support customer authentication and
authorization. Entra External ID supports advanced authentication workflows and includes social
identity providers such as Facebook and Google out of the box.
Niche players such as Auth0/Okta and Ping/ForgeRock are among the most advanced solutions in
the CIAM world. ForgeRock has an impressive offering and can accommodate nearly any authen -
tication workflow. It also integrates with HSMs (Azure Dedicated HSM or your own on-premises
HSM), which is particularly useful to sign JWT tokens and Security Assertion Markup Language
(SAML) assertions since the private keys used to sign such tokens never leave the boundaries of
the HSM.
Introducing authentication, authorization, and Conditional
Access policies
The terms authentication and authorization are often confused—partly because certain features
straddle both domains.
Authentication is the process whereby a user submits credentials to an identity provider, which
then verifies them. Once successfully validated, the user is signed in.
Authorization determines whether a user or application has permission to access a particular
resource. It’s the responsibility of the resource server to allow or deny access.
This distinction can become blurred with features such as Conditional Access, which intersects
both processes.
For instance, during user sign-in, Conditional Access might prompt for Multi-Factor Authen -
tication (MFA) based on specific conditions (such as login attempts from unfamiliar locations),
but it can also serve as an access gatekeeper—deciding, for example, whether a user can enter
the Azure portal depending on preconfigured rules. Blocking access is more part of the authori -
zation realm than the authentication one. Conditional Access can be seen as the policy engine of
a zero-trust security model that makes decisions based on signals received from devices, users,
networks, and locations.
All of this can contribute to confusion between authentication and authorization.
Security Architecture 338
The Identity Protection feature protects against malicious authentication activities. Figure 9.7
illustrates the different features made available by Identity Protection:
Figure 9.7 – Identity Protection

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 339
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 339
Identity Protection is mostly useful for detecting three types of risks: user, sign-in, and workload
identity risks.
A user risk means that the user might have been compromised. A sign-in risk is identified while
the user signs in. A workload identity risk means that a service principal (non-human user) might
have been compromised.
By combining risk detection with CAPs, we can prevent potentially compromised users or appli -
cations from accessing specific resources. CAPs allow us to define powerful rules. For example,
very common rules that can be defined are the following:
• Triggering MFA when accessing specific resources
• Location-based policies, such as either requiring MFA or denying/granting access based
on the user’s location
• Requiring full re-authentication for risk-based policies
• Enforcing the use of corporate devices only
• Triggering MFA if a low/medium sign-in risk is identified
• Blocking access in case a high user, sign-in, or workload identity risk is identified
All these policies typically end up with either blocking or granting access, or triggering MFA.
For example, if you run a business in a specific country or a handful of countries, you may block
all locations except the ones you’re active in. The following is a real-world-inspired policy that
had to comply with the following rules:
• Access to all apps except Azure DevOps and Microsoft Azure Management was blocked
when coming from outside of Belgium and the Netherlands
• Locations such as India and Morocco were allowed for the two exempted apps because
some specific tasks were outsourced
Security Architecture 340
These rules correspond to the policy illustrated in Figure 9.8:
Figure 9.8 – Blocking access from non-whitelisted countries with Conditional Access
As you can see in Figure 9.8, there is also the possibility to enable the policy in report mode. This
is particularly convenient to observe the behavior of a policy once activated and make sure you
didn’t make any configuration mistakes, as it directly impacts the login experience and may cause
trouble for end users. Another possibility is to have a non-production tenant (a separate instance
of Entra ID) where you can test those policies.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 341
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 341
An additional authentication-related feature is Smart Lockout, which helps prevent brute-force
attacks by only locking the account after a configurable number of failed attempts, and by im -
posing a configurable time interval across login attempts.
Lastly, Entra ID has a few passwordless options and integrates seamlessly with FIDO2/passkeys,
the Microsoft Authenticator app, as well as Temporary Access Pass (TAP) and QR code-based
authentication. TAP allows you to register passwordless authentication methods.
In terms of authorization, Entra ID has directory-specific roles, such as Application Developer,
Application Administrator, and Global Administrator, which all allow you to manage and config -
ure Entra ID. For any Azure-related resources, we rely on Azure RBAC, which features hundreds
of roles. It is important to consider the Azure hierarchy that we described in Chapter 2, Solution
Architecture, since it is where we apply RBAC permissions and policies. We’ll tackle other autho -
rization-specific aspects in the next section.
Introducing common protocols such as OIDC, OAuth 2.0,
and SAML
SAML is a widely recognized legacy protocol that remains in active use today, particularly in fed -
eration scenarios. However, cloud-native applications typically rely on OAuth 2.0 and OpenID
Connect (OIDC), and newer federation implementations are increasingly adopting OIDC. As such,
our focus will be exclusively on OAuth 2.0 and OIDC. That said, it’s important to acknowledge
that SAML continues to play a role and is expected to persist for the foreseeable future.
Both OAuth 2.0 and OIDC are international standards and are not specific to Azure. In this section,
we will examine how Entra ID supports these protocols, noting that its implementation does not
fully align with the specifications in all aspects.
Security Architecture 342
Before diving deeper into endpoints, tokens, and authorization flows, it’s important to first un -
derstand the key actors involved when using OIDC with Entra ID.
Figure 9.9 – OIDC actors with Entra ID
Figure 9.9 shows three main actors:
• The identity and authorization server: In Figure 9.9, Entra ID plays both roles. Note
that it is rather common to split those roles into two distinct services. For example, you
may use Entra External ID for authentication and Keycloak or Duende for authorization.
• The business application: This can be anything that uses either a public or confidential
client application. We’ll explain these different types of applications later. In any case, the
business service will have to use a client application for which a corresponding applica -
tion object exists in Entra ID. This requires the registration of the client application prior
to its use. In Entra ID, we can grant permissions over resources to the client application.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 341
chunks.content:
• The resource server: This can, for example, be a backend service that is exposed as an
API. This resource server must have a corresponding resource identifier in Entra ID. This
is typically achieved by registering an application that represents the resource server and
that exposes an API. We can optionally expose custom roles and scopes. The resource server
must perform the token validation to ensure the calling client is legitimate.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 343
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 343
Note that Entra ID allows us to use a single application object to represent both the client and
the resource, but this is rather considered bad practice to club them and would only make sense
when the client and the resource share the same lifecycle.
Whenever a business application requests a token, Entra ID verifies that both the client applica -
tion and the target resource (resource server) are registered and recognized. It also ensures that
the request complies with the specific requirements of the OAuth flow being used by the calling
application.
Now that the fundamentals are in place, let’s explore the broader OIDC landscape.
Figure 9.10 illustrates the vast world of OIDC, which is a layer on top of OAuth 2.0:
Figure 9.10 – OIDC map
Important note
To have a better view of this map, you can download the PDF file available at https://
github.com/PacktPublishing/The-Azure-Cloud-Native-Architecture-
Mapbook-Second-Edition/blob/main/Chapter09/maps/oidc.pdf
Security Architecture 344
Figure 9.10 provides a generic overview of OIDC’s capabilities. It includes warning symbols to draw
attention to specific considerations or limitations relevant to Entra ID, which will be detailed in
the following sections.
The five dimensions we’re going to explore are shown in Figure 9.11:
Figure 9.11 – OIDC dimensions
Let’s start with the Endpoints section.
Understanding OIDC endpoints and mapping them to Entra ID
Any OIDC interaction must go through one of the endpoints illustrated in Figure 9.12:

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 345
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 345
Figure 9.12 – Entra ID endpoints for OIDC
The Discovery endpoint is a well-known URL that exposes configuration metadata necessary for
clients to integrate with Entra ID. The endpoint looks as follows:
https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration.
This endpoint returns a document that outlines Entra ID’s capabilities. It essentially serves as a
directory of the available endpoints and includes the location of the public keys—exposed via
the jwks_uri attribute—that can be used to verify the signatures of tokens issued by Entra ID.
We’ll come back to token validation practices later on.
The Authorization endpoint handles things such as user consent, meaning when a client ap -
plication has requested access to a resource on behalf of a user (resource owner). Upon user
consent, it typically returns an authorization code, which can be reused by the client for further
token acquisition. This allows a client application to interact with a resource on your behalf. In
Entra ID, we usually skip the user consent by letting an administrator consent on behalf of the
entire organization.
Security Architecture 346
The Token endpoint is used by client applications to request all types of tokens, among which
are refresh tokens, which we will explain in the next section. When a human user is involved,
the first step is usually to first leverage the authorization endpoint, then connect to the token
endpoint, and exchange the authorization code for an access token. When the client application
needs a token for itself (as an app with no user involved), it typically requests the access token
directly from the token endpoint.
The Introspection endpoint doesn’t exist in Entra ID. It is linked to reference tokens, which we
will explain in the next section. It’s an important limitation of Entra.
The Revocation endpoint is typically used to revoke both refresh and reference tokens, but in
the case of Entra ID, it can only revoke refresh tokens.
The Device Authorization endpoint is used in situations where the client device, such as a smart
TV, doesn’t have a (decent) browser or UI that allows for an easy experience. The user authen -
ticates and can enter a device code sent by Entra ID using another device than the one that is
originally requesting access.
Last but not least, the UserInfo endpoint allows client applications to retrieve additional infor -
mation about the logged-in user.
Be aware that other SAML-specific endpoints are also exposed by Entra ID. Now, let’s look at the
different token types and highlight some other Entra ID limitations.
Understanding token types, lifetime, revocation, and Entra ID
limitations
We already slightly introduced token types in Chapter 6, Developing and Designing Applications
with Azure, but we’ll provide a broader coverage in this section. Let’s start by exploring the dif -

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 345
chunks.content:
ferent token types.
Figure 9.13 illustrates the different token types that exist in OIDC:

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 347
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 347
Figure 9.13 – Token types
Here is an explanation of the four token types:
• ID tokens: These contain user-related information. They are mostly used in client applica -
tions, such as Single-Page Applications (SPAs) or mobile apps. ID tokens typically contain
claims such as preferred_name or email. They may also contain a pointer to the groups a
given user belongs to. ID tokens should never be used outside of the business application’s
client interface. In other words, they are not meant to be used for API or resource access.
• Access tokens: These represent a credential issued by an authorization server (for exam -
ple, Entra ID) that allows the client application to access resources, such as custom and
third-party APIs, on behalf of the logged-in user or as an application. With Entra ID, access
tokens are not opaque but self-contained value tokens. This means that any entity in posses -
sion of a valid access token can access the resource for which it was issued, regardless of
how the token was obtained. As an analogy, an access token is like a set of house keys:
you don’t need to be the owner to enter—if you have the keys and know where the house
is, you can get inside. Access tokens cannot be revoked in Entra ID.
Security Architecture 348
It is therefore important to consider their lifetime. It’s worth noting that Entra ID supports
Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) based on the OpenID Continuous Access Evalua -
tion Profile (CAEP), allowing your applications and APIs to respond to critical events such
as password changes or account disablement—provided they are CAE-aware themselves.
More on this here: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/
app-resilience-continuous-access-evaluation.
• Refresh tokens: These are long-lived credentials used to obtain new access tokens on
behalf of the authenticated user. They play a key role in avoiding repeated user authen -
tication when access tokens expire, which is especially beneficial for mobile applications
and browser-based clients. However, due to their extended lifespan and critical role in
maintaining session continuity, exposing refresh tokens in public clients poses significant
security risks. A recommended best practice is to implement the Backend for Frontend
(BFF) pattern (described in the next section), which ensures that all token handling re -
mains on the server side, preventing any type of token from being exposed to the client. A
few Entra ID events (changing password, user disabled, etc.) may revoke existing refresh
tokens depending on whether they are used by confidential or public clients. Adminis -
trators can, however, enforce a refresh token revocation for a given user, which applies
to all client types.
• Reference tokens: These are opaque access tokens and they are not supported in Entra ID.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 347
chunks.content:
They act as a pointer to the authorization server. The benefit of using such tokens is that
they can be revoked at any point in time. The APIs receiving such tokens cannot validate
them directly and must call the authorization server’s introspection endpoint. This type
of endpoint doesn’t exist in Entra ID. Be aware that even if Entra ID did support them,
using this type of token would introduce a performance penalty and would require a
highly scalable authorization server, since it would have to handle many more requests.
Alternatives to Entra ID, such as Duende and Keycloak, support reference tokens. However,
they might be more useful in CIAM scenarios, where you may use Entra External ID for
authentication and Duende or Keycloak for authorization.
It is worth noting that the token lifetime also depends on the scenario and the identity that is
used to request a token. Here are the different types of identities available in Entra ID:

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 349
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 349
• Registered applications: This type of object is explicitly registered, either to expose and
secure a custom API or to enable API access for client applications. The registration pro -
cess depends on whether the application is intended for use by a public or a confidential
client. When assigning permissions, we differentiate between delegated and application
permissions. Delegated permissions allow the client application to access a resource
(for example, the Graph API) on behalf of the signed-in user, provided that the user or
an administrator has granted consent. This type of app often requires a client secret or
a client certificate, depending on the chosen authorization flow. Be aware that using a
client certificate is considered more secure but adds some extra constraints for the busi -
ness application using the client app. The token lifetime is one hour by default but can be
modified through specific policies. This type of application also benefits from enterprise
features such as the possibility to restrict its use to specific users and groups and map
group memberships to custom API roles.
• Managed identities: This type of object is provisioned by Azure. In practice, we create
Azure resources that are given either system-assigned or user-assigned managed identities,
which automatically results in the creation of a corresponding service principal in Entra
ID. When these managed identities are used to obtain access tokens, the tokens have a
fixed lifetime of 24 hours. This duration cannot be altered. The reason is that applications
using managed identities do not communicate directly with Entra ID’s token endpoint.
Instead, they interact with a local endpoint provided by Azure on the Azure service (for
example, app service, virtual machine, and so on). This local endpoint caches tokens for
24 hours, and there is no supported policy mechanism to override this behavior. Note that
the use of managed identities is mostly restricted to accessing Azure resources such as an
Azure SQL database or a Service Bus instance. It is technically possible to use managed
identities to consume custom APIs, but it is not so common in practice.
• Workload identity federation through user-assigned identities: This type of identity
allows you to establish trust between an external system, such as AKS or GitHub, and En -
tra ID. The external system becomes a token issuer whose tokens can be exchanged with
Entra ID tokens through federated identities materialized using user-assigned managed
identities. As a consequence, the token lifetime is also 24 hours. As for managed identities,
we typically use federation through user-assigned identities to access Azure resources
and leverage the Azure RBAC model to grant permissions.
• Workload identity federation through app registration: This type of identity allows you

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 349
chunks.content:
to establish trust between an external system and Entra ID, but the way they integrate
is through an app registration. As a consequence, the token lifetime defaults to one hour
and can be adjusted using custom policies.
Security Architecture 350
While leveraging both managed identities and workload identities is considered a best practice,
the fixed lifetime of the resulting access tokens can raise concerns. Nevertheless, these types of
identities are widely adopted due to their convenience when accessing Azure-only resources.
Infrastructure as code pipelines do not require direct interaction with Entra ID—they only need
to provision user-assigned identities, which automatically result in corresponding service princi -
pals. In contrast, using app registrations instead of user-assigned identities introduces scalability
challenges; they require direct access to Entra ID and support only up to 20 federated credentials
per application, but one of the greatest benefits is that they can be used with Conditional Access,
unlike the other methods. So, it might be a good option for some specific scenarios.
In Kubernetes environments such as AKS, where hundreds or thousands of Pods may exist, ad -
hering to the least-privilege principle would necessitate a large number of app registrations—an
approach that does not scale effectively.
Grasping the different authorization flows and token acquisition
mechanisms
It is essential to identify which authorization flow is appropriate for each type of application. Many
developers and security professionals lack a clear understanding of how these flows should be
used, which can easily result in security vulnerabilities and the leak of tokens/secrets.
As we highlighted earlier, the notion of public and confidential clients is important. Public cli -
ents are applications that cannot securely store credentials or client secrets. For example, a web
browser can store data in its web storage (session or local storage) but the information is easily
accessible by anyone with access to the device. In the case of a web browser, malicious JavaScript
code can also easily be injected and access that sensitive information. Similarly, mobile apps,
user laptops, and so on are considered public clients as their owner/user can typically extract the
information. It is, therefore, important not to store a shared secret on such devices. An example
of a shared secret might be the secret obtained during the app registration process or an API key,
or even the root key of a storage account.
Conversely, confidential clients are server-side components that can easily store secrets and that
are managed by infrastructure administrators. For example, a custom backend service could store
a secret in Azure Key Vault and pull it at runtime using its managed identity. The secret cannot

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 349
chunks.content:
be seen directly by the end user.
The type of authorization flow we can use depends on the type of client used by the business
application. Technically, there is nothing preventing the use of a confidential client on an end
user device.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 351
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 351
For example, you could embed a client ID and client secret in a mobile app package and use it from
a mobile device. However, such credentials could easily be extracted through package inspection
or traffic capture. It is, therefore, the responsibility of security analysts and architects to assess
and mitigate the associated risks.
Figure 9.14 illustrates the different flows available in OIDC:
Figure 9.14 – Authorization flows
Public clients, such as SPAs, historically relied on the Implicit Grant flow. However, due to its
security vulnerabilities, this flow is now deprecated and should be avoided. It may still be en -
countered in legacy applications. The recommended alternative for public clients is the Proof
Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) flow, which offers stronger protection by introducing a dynam -
ically generated secret to mitigate interception attacks. PKCE is used together with a secretless
Authorization Code flow.
For Model-View-Controller (MVC) applications, which are considered confidential clients, sev -
eral authorization flows are available. The Authorization Code flow relies on a pair of credentials
(client ID and client secret) that can be securely stored on the server side and, as its name indicates,
returns an authorization code to the client, which can then be exchanged for tokens.
Security Architecture 352
When an ID token is needed during the initial interaction with the authorization server, one option
is the Hybrid flow—a combination of the deprecated Implicit Grant and the Authorization Code
flow—or, preferably, the more secure PKCE in combination with the Authorization Code flow.
In short, the PKCE flow is recommended for all clients, whether public or confidential.
For machine-to-machine or service-to-service interactions, the most commonly used flow is the
Client Credentials flow. It relies on a pair of credentials—a client ID and a client secret—which is
appropriate for confidential clients. The flow is straightforward, involving a single HTTP request
to the token endpoint to obtain an access token.
A more secure variant uses a client ID in combination with a client certificate instead of a secret.
In this approach, the public key of the certificate must be uploaded to the application registered
in Entra ID. The client application then generates a client assertion—a JWT token signed with its
private key—to authenticate itself. This method is considered more secure because it leverages
asymmetric cryptography: the private key stays with the client, while only the public key is shared
with Entra ID, avoiding the risks associated with shared secrets. An even more secure version
of the Client Credentials flow is to use certificate-bound access tokens, which include certificate
information inside the token, but this is not supported by Entra.

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 351
chunks.content:
An additional machine-to-machine flow is Resource Owner Password Grant, which is discour -
aged but still used in situations where a resource does not support the Client Credentials flow
and the resource consumer does not have a human user. For example, the consumer could be a
background job that must interact with a resource with the equivalent of a service account. In
that case, the service account is like a user, but the username and password are used by a machine
instead of a human.
Lastly, the Device Code flow is designed for devices that do not have a browser or have very limited
UI capabilities. The device sends a request to Entra ID, waits for a code to display to the user, and
then repeatedly polls the token endpoint with the received code until the user is authenticated,
after which an access token is returned to the device.
You can easily watch this flow in action by sniffing the traffic of the az login --use-device-
code command.
Using PKCE for public clients is important, but it’s not the only consideration. You also need to
decide whether tokens should be returned directly to the client device. For years, SPAs and mobile
apps were typically designed to receive tokens directly from the authorization server. However, in
recent years, the BFF pattern—originally intended to serve client-specific needs—has emerged

chunks.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 353
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 353
as a preferred approach. It acts as an intermediary, helping to keep tokens off the client device
and enhancing security by limiting exposure.
Figure 9.15 illustrates the BFF pattern used for requesting and managing tokens on behalf of
client devices:
Figure 9.15 – BFF pattern with OIDC
Be aware that most application teams push back on this implementation as they see this as a
constraint. A potential trade-off consists of enforcing the BFF pattern for any internet-facing
asset and possibly allowing user tokens to surface in public clients for internal and corporate
apps. The risks encountered in letting tokens go back to the client are mostly linked to JavaS -
cript-based (cross-site scripting, etc.) and Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks. Note that while
the cookie-based approach protects against JavaScript-based attacks (providing the cookie is set
to HttpOnly), it does not protect against MITM.
Security Architecture 354
Scalability is another key consideration when implementing the BFF pattern. In a traditional setup
without a BFF, tokens are managed and stored locally on each client device, effectively distributing
the storage across all users. In contrast, introducing a BFF centralizes token management, requiring
server-side storage for all active sessions. This typically necessitates a distributed cache such as
Redis, along with proper session cleanup mechanisms. Additionally, placing a BFF between the
client and the target resource introduces extra latency. As with any architectural choice, adopting
BFF involves trade-offs between security, scalability, and performance.
Next, we’ll see how to perform proper token validation and clarify the role of scopes, which is
often misunderstood.
Getting up to speed with token validation and access control
mechanisms
Token validation is an important task that should be correctly understood.
There are two schools of thought: those who believe that relying solely on an API gateway without
additional validation in the backend code is sufficient, and those who believe the backend should
always validate the token, regardless of the architecture in place. I belong to the latter. I think it is
important to always validate the token in the code because the backend represents the resource
server. The gateway is useful to stop illegal requests earlier, but you should not rely only on the
gateway. Moreover, any change in the architecture could expose the backend.
However, by default, application code does not enforce any token validation. It is the responsibility
of developers to implement proper validation logic to ensure the received tokens are correctly
verified. In my experience conducting numerous API audits, I have consistently encountered se -
curity flaws—such as unprotected API operations or entire controllers lacking the proper access
